Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event
The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A medical-equipment visual trigger is hard to reconcile as a central combat-related trigger for this profile, especially alongside otherwise combat-consistent threat items and without any medical/hospital-related memory or appraisal content. It suggests a different trauma context and is clinically difficult to integrate with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense rage on recall conflicts with the paired reports of emotionally numb recall and the memory feeling alien/detached. Fluctuation can occur, but as a compact three-item profile these items pull in opposing directions—high emotional arousal versus marked dissociative detachment—without other memory content to bridge them.

Memory: Rage on Recall + Emotionless Recall + Memory Feels Alien

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Rage on Recall' conflicts with the paired endorsement of markedly detached recall ('Emotionless Recall' and 'Memory Feels Alien'). Intense rage during recall and recall experienced as numb/alien can both occur in PTSD, but selecting all three as coequal memory descriptors creates a direct within-node tension between highly affect-laden remembering and strongly depersonalized, affectless remembering. The rest of the profile coherently reflects severe combat-related PTSD, but this specific Memory combination is the main clinically questionable inconsistency.

issues.item: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, two items describe markedly detached/derealized recall ('emotionless', 'belongs to someone else') while another describes intensely affect-laden reliving ('same terror I felt at the time'). These can both occur across different moments in PTSD, but as the only three selected memory items they pull in opposing directions and are not a clean, internally coherent depiction of a single dominant memory style for this profile.

These two appraisals are plausible in severe PTSD, but for a 63-year-old married airline pilot they create a hard-to-explain mismatch with the rest of the profile when presented without any trauma-linked appraisal content. 'I have no future' is especially discordant for an older, still-employed patient and is not well integrated with the combat-specific trigger/threat pattern. The Negative Appraisals node is dominated by global depressive identity/future statements rather than trauma-related meanings that would plausibly connect to the very strong Triggers → Negative Appraisals edge in the formulation.

vignette:
Sione is a 63-year-old airline pilot, a married American man of Pacific Islander background, who came to treatment after admitting that the cockpit had begun to feel less like a workplace than a place where he was bracing for something to break through. Decades earlier, during combat, he had been in a night operation that turned chaotic after a helicopter came under attack on landing. He remembers the hard vibration of the aircraft, the whine of rotors overhead, men shouting in the dark, and then being pressed against rough webbing and canvas inside the aircraft while waiting to move. What remains most vivid is not a coherent sequence but fragments that still strike with the force of the original moment: the sound of helicopter blades, the particular scratch of military fabric against his hands, and the darkness at that same hour of night when he believed he might die.

In the years since, Sione has often said the memory does not feel fully like his, as if it belongs to someone else and yet can overtake him without warning. When it comes back, it is not experienced as a distant recollection but with the same terror he felt then. A passing helicopter, the coarse texture of certain seat fabrics or webbed materials, or simply being awake at that time of night can pull the whole scene into the present in an instant. Because the memory arrives so suddenly and so completely, he has come to live as though danger can emerge anywhere; he scans for exits as soon as he enters a room, startles sharply when someone moves suddenly near him, and feels distinctly less safe after dark.

Those reactions have become especially difficult in his working life. As a pilot, he cannot avoid aircraft noise, and on the tarmac the thudding approach of rotor blades from airport service helicopters can make his body tense before he has fully registered why. In crew lounges and terminals, he automatically notes every door and alternate route out. If a gate agent or co-pilot shifts abruptly at his side, he is instantly on guard. Night flights are the hardest. The time of day itself seems loaded for him, and once that evening hour approaches, his sense that the world is dangerous becomes less like a thought and more like the atmosphere he is breathing. The trigger and the vigilance feed each other: the more keyed up he is, the more quickly he catches the sound of aircraft overhead, the feel of rough upholstery beneath his hand, the onset of darkness, and each of those cues confirms for him that he is right to stay watchful.

Over time, Sione has built a painful understanding of himself around these experiences. He has come to believe there is something wrong with him as a person, that other men moved on from war and he somehow did not. When a helicopter passes and he feels his chest tighten, he does not only fear danger; he also reads his own reaction as proof that he is damaged. He often says he used to be a happy person and is now simply miserable, as though the war stripped something essential out of him. The memory’s strange quality—both alien and overwhelmingly real—deepens that judgment. If his own past can feel foreign and still reduce him to terror, he takes this as evidence that he is fundamentally defective. From there, his guard goes up even further: if he is not sound, and the world is dangerous, then it feels necessary to keep watching, especially at night and wherever there is no clear exit.

That same belief system makes the triggers more potent. He listens for aircraft sounds because part of him expects the world to prove itself dangerous again. He notices the rough textures that echo the aircraft interior because he is already braced for signs that something is wrong, outside and inside him. In turn, his constant scanning and readiness seem to prime the memory. A room entered by instinctively locating the exits becomes a room organized around threat, and in that state the combat scene is closer to the surface. A sudden movement by another person can bring back not just alarm but the full bodily sense of that night, and once the memory surges in, his conviction hardens that happiness is gone for good and that danger is the truest fact about the world.

What finally brought Sione in was not a single episode but the realization that he was structuring his life around surviving reminders. His wife had noticed that he was most unreachable in the evenings, pacing the house, checking locks, and seeming elsewhere even when he was present. At work he remained highly competent, but he was exhausted by the strain of staying composed while feeling ambushed by sounds, textures, and darkness. He is seeking help now because he is afraid that if this continues, the terror will keep colonizing more of his life. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget the war, but to have the memory feel like his own past instead of something waiting in the environment to seize him again.
